title: Econ 22003: Principles of Microeconomics
text:
Prerequisites:
Math 1203 or higher, or a score of 26 on math part of ACT exam or 600 on math part of SAT exam.

title: Econ 22003: Principles of Microeconomics
text:
Course Description:
The course introduces students to economics way of thinking to study households’ and firms’behavior and their interaction in markets and its effect on resource allocation. Both consumer andproducer behavior will be analyzed. Topics include, among others, the determination of pricesunder different market structures, elasticity and the effects of government policies in markets.

title: Econ 22003: Principles of Microeconomics
section: Learning Objectives: By the end of the course, the student should be able to:
text:
Learning Objectives: By the end of the course, the student should be able to:
By the end of the course, the student should be able to: + Explain how supply and demand determine price and quantities of a good and theimplication of this for efficient allocation of resources. + Explain the concept of elasticity and its applications in pricing and policy. + Evaluate the efficiency of markets in allocating resources and the conditions necessary forperfect competition to exist. + Examine different market structures, including monopolies, oligopolies, and monopolisticcompetition, and analyze their implications for market outcomes. + Discuss the role of government in regulating markets. + Analyze the theory of production and cost, including short-run and long-run decision-making by firms. + Apply microeconomic principles to real-world scenarios, such as pricing strategies, marketinterventions, and policy analysis, to develop critical thinking and problem-solving skills.

title: Econ 22003: Principles of Microeconomics
text:
Value of the Course:
The course will provide students with a basic understanding of macroeconomic concepts critical to informed decision making, whether as a consumer, businessperson, voter, or policymaker.

title: Econ 22003: Principles of Microeconomics
text:
Class Procedures:
This class is fully in person. Class will consist primarily of lectures and demonstrations, with students’ questions and participation in discussions greatly encouraged.

title: Principles of Macroeconomics
text:
Prerequisites:
Math 1203 or higher, or a score of 26 on math part of ACT exam or 600 on math part of SAT exam.

title: Principles of Macroeconomics
text:
Course Description:
The course is an introduction to economic issues on the national and international level and the tools to analyze them. The course discusses various economic models of aggregate economic indicators such as national income, inflation and unemployment. It also addresses how these aggregates can be altered by monetary and fiscal policies.

title: Principles of Macroeconomics
section: Learning Objectives: By the end of the course, the student should be able to:
text:
Learning Objectives: By the end of the course, the student should be able to:

Describe the concepts and measurement of gross domestic product, unemployment and inflation and the models used to explain and predict these variables.
Explain the difference between business cycle and economic growth and the factors that contribute to each.
Demonstrate how Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply determine equilibrium price level, output and employment in the short-run and long-run.
Describe the multiplier concept, how it is computed, and its qualifications and limitations.
Explain the concepts, tools, and implementation of fiscal and Monetary policies, each policy’s limitations and relative advantages/disadvantages, and how each affects aggregate economic activity.

title: Can quantum-mechanical description of physical reality be considered complete?
text:
Abstract
In a complete theory there is an element corresponding to each element of reality. A sufficient condition for the reality of a physical quantity is the possibility of predicting it with certainty, without disturbing the system. In quantum mechanics in the case of two physical quantities described by non-commuting operators, the knowledge of one precludes the knowledge of the other. Then either (1) the description of reality given by the wave function in quantum mechanics is not complete or (2) these two quantities cannot have simultaneous reality. Consideration of the problem of making predictions concerning a system on the basis of measurements made on another system that had previously interacted with it leads to the result that if (1) is false then (2) is also false. One is thus led to conclude that the description of reality as given by a wave function is not complete.
